name: Florence
tagline: Renaissance genius, Tuscan wine and terracotta rooftops
description:
Florence packs more Renaissance brilliance into a walkable square mile than most countries manage in total. Brunelleschi's terracotta dome still anchors every skyline view, Botticelli's goddesses drift through the Uffizi, and Michelangelo's David stands in marble-veined confidence a few streets away. Yet the city is no museum piece: Vespas buzz along the Arno, butchers banter across the stalls of San Lorenzo, and artisans still gild frames and stitch leather in Oltrarno workshops handed down through generations.

The secret to loving Florence is pacing. Book the headline galleries for early morning, then spend afternoons drifting across the river, where Santo Spirito's piazza fills with aperitivo crowds and trattorias serve ribollita and bistecca on paper tablecloths. Climb to Piazzale Michelangelo or San Miniato for sunset, when the whole city glows the colour of ripe apricots.

Florence is also the perfect launchpad for Tuscany. Chianti's vineyards are under an hour away, and Siena, Pisa and Lucca are easy day trips, so four or five days lets you balance art-heavy mornings with lazy wine-country escapes.

safety.notes: Violent crime is rare, but pickpockets work the crowds around the Duomo, Santa Maria Novella station and packed buses. Keep phones off café tables and ignore anyone pushing 'free' bracelets or petitions.

tipping: A cover charge (coperto) is common and service is sometimes included; otherwise rounding up or leaving 5–10% for good service is appreciated but never expected.
gettingAround: The historic centre is compact and best explored on foot; the T2 tram links the airport to Santa Maria Novella station in about 20 minutes, and regional trains and buses reach Pisa, Lucca and Siena in 60–90 minutes.
tips: Reserve timed tickets for the Uffizi, the Accademia and the Duomo dome climb weeks ahead in high season; walk-up queues can swallow half a day.
Drink your espresso standing at the bar — the same coffee costs two or three times as much at a table on a big piazza.
Refill your bottle for free at the city's public 'fontanelli' water kiosks, several of which even dispense chilled sparkling water.
Never drive into the ZTL limited-traffic zone: cameras log every plate, and rental companies forward the fines months after you get home.
Most state museums close on Mondays, so save that day for markets, the Oltrarno workshops or a Chianti day trip.
Florence's tourist tax (up to about €8 per person per night at top hotels) is collected at check-out, so budget for it on top of the room rate.
etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees to enter churches, including the Duomo — guards really do turn people away.
Greet shop staff with 'buongiorno' or 'buonasera' when you walk in; skipping it comes across as rude.
Sitting or eating on church steps and monuments is banned in parts of the centre and can earn an on-the-spot fine.
Italians rarely order cappuccino after late morning or with a meal; an espresso after dinner is the done thing.

neighborhoods.name: Centro Storico
neighborhoods.blurb: The UNESCO-listed core around the Duomo and Piazza della Signoria, where nearly every major sight is within a 15-minute stroll. Heaving by day, surprisingly hushed after 11pm.

neighborhoods.name: Santo Spirito
neighborhoods.blurb: The Oltrarno's bohemian heart, with a plain-fronted Brunelleschi church, a piazza ringed by bars and a monthly flea market. Students and local families keep it grounded.

neighborhoods.name: San Frediano
neighborhoods.blurb: A former weavers' quarter now packed with natural-wine bars, craft studios and some of the best-value trattorias in the city.

neighborhoods.name: Sant'Ambrogio
neighborhoods.blurb: East of Santa Croce and anchored by a genuine neighbourhood market where Florentines do their daily shop. Great for cheap lunches and picnic supplies.

neighborhoods.name: San Niccolò
neighborhoods.blurb: A tiny riverside enclave beneath the hill to Piazzale Michelangelo, with a medieval gate tower, wine bars and a village feel minutes from the centre.

dishes.name: Bistecca alla fiorentina
dishes.description: A towering T-bone grilled over embers, seasoned with nothing but salt and served rosy-rare. It's priced by weight, and one steak easily feeds two.

dishes.name: Lampredotto
dishes.description: The cow's fourth stomach, slow-simmered with tomato and herbs, then stuffed into a crusty roll with green sauce and chilli oil — Florence's signature street snack.

dishes.name: Ribollita
dishes.description: A thick 'reboiled' soup of cavolo nero, cannellini beans and day-old Tuscan bread, finished with a generous slick of peppery new-season olive oil.

dishes.name: Schiacciata
dishes.description: Salty, olive-oil-soaked flatbread split and piled with finocchiona salami, pecorino or porchetta for a cheap and very filling lunch.

dishes.name: Cantucci e Vin Santo
dishes.description: Crunchy almond biscuits dunked into amber, raisin-sweet Vin Santo — the traditional way to close a Tuscan meal.

events.name: Scoppio del Carro
events.description: On Easter Sunday a towering antique cart packed with fireworks is set off in front of the Duomo by a dove-shaped rocket, a ritual said to foretell a good harvest.

events.name: Maggio Musicale Fiorentino
events.description: Italy's oldest music festival fills the Teatro del Maggio with opera, symphonic concerts and ballet from late spring into early summer.

events.name: Calcio Storico Fiorentino
events.description: Four historic neighbourhood teams clash in a brutal mix of rugby, wrestling and football on sand in Piazza Santa Croce, with the final on 24 June for the feast of San Giovanni.

events.name: Festa della Rificolona
events.description: On the evening of 7 September children parade glowing paper lanterns through the streets to Piazza Santissima Annunziata, where a fair of farm produce fills the square.

attractions.name: Florence Cathedral
attractions.description: Brunelleschi's colossal brick dome, raised without a forest of ground scaffolding, is the engineering feat that kick-started the Renaissance. The interior is surprisingly austere, but climbing 463 steps between the dome's inner and outer shells brings you face to face with Vasari's Last Judgment frescoes and out onto a sea of terracotta rooftops.
attractions.bookingTip: Entry to the cathedral is free, but the dome, bell tower and baptistery need a Brunelleschi Pass with a timed dome slot — book a week ahead in summer.

attractions.name: Uffizi
attractions.description: Room after room of the world's greatest Renaissance collection unfolds along a U-shaped corridor overlooking the Arno: Botticelli's Birth of Venus, Leonardo's Annunciation, Titian's Venus of Urbino and Caravaggio's snake-haired Medusa. Pace yourself — two hours of focused looking beats four hours of museum fatigue.
attractions.bookingTip: Reserve a timed ticket online for the 08:15 slot; without one, the summer queue can top two hours.

attractions.name: Ponte Vecchio
attractions.description: The only Florentine bridge spared in the Second World War is lined with tiny jewellers' shops cantilevered over the water, a tradition dating back to when the Medici evicted the smelly butchers in favour of goldsmiths. Look up to trace the Vasari Corridor, the dukes' private elevated walkway, running along the top.
attractions.bookingTip: Come after 21:00 when the shutters are down and the bridge is nearly empty, or photograph it at sunset from neighbouring Ponte Santa Trinita.

attractions.name: Galleria dell'Accademia
attractions.description: Michelangelo's David stands at the end of a skylit tribune, more than five metres of flawless marble that looks startlingly alive up close. Don't rush past the unfinished Prisoners lining the approach — their half-carved bodies seem to wrestle their way out of the stone.
attractions.bookingTip: Book the first or the last entry slot of the day; late-afternoon visitors often get the David almost to themselves.

attractions.name: Palazzo Vecchio
attractions.description: The fortress-like town hall still houses Florence's mayor, but its museum rooms show off Medici power at full volume, from the gilded Hall of the Five Hundred to hidden doors concealed behind painted wall maps. Climb the Arnolfo Tower for the best close-up view of the Duomo's dome.
attractions.bookingTip: Add the small-group 'secret passages' visit when you book — spots are limited and it unlocks hidden stairways and the Medici's jewel-box study.

attractions.name: Piazzale Michelangelo
attractions.description: This broad terrace on the south bank delivers the definitive Florence panorama: the dome, Palazzo Vecchio's tower and a procession of bridges stacked along the Arno. Walk ten minutes higher to the Romanesque church of San Miniato al Monte, where monks chant Gregorian vespers most evenings.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive 45 minutes before sunset to claim a spot on the steps, and walk up the garden ramps from San Niccolò instead of taking a taxi.

attractions.name: Palazzo Pitti
attractions.description: The Medici's vast rusticated-stone palace hides several museums, including the Palatine Gallery, whose walls are hung floor-to-ceiling with Raphaels and Titians, and the lavish royal apartments later used by Italy's kings. It sees a fraction of the Uffizi's crowds, making it a calmer art fix.
attractions.bookingTip: If you plan to see the Uffizi, Pitti and Boboli, the multi-day PassePartout ticket covers all three for less than separate entries.

attractions.name: Boboli Gardens
attractions.description: Rising behind Palazzo Pitti, the Medici's formal gardens climb past grottoes dripping with fake stalactites, cypress avenues and a stone amphitheatre to a hilltop porcelain museum with sweeping views of olive-clad hills. Bring water and decent shoes — the gravel slopes are steeper than they look.
attractions.hours: 08:15–18:30 in summer, to 16:30 in winter; closed 1st and last Mon of the month
attractions.bookingTip: Go at opening on hot days, as the upper terraces have almost no shade by noon.

attractions.name: Basilica of Santa Croce
attractions.description: Often called Italy's pantheon, this vast Franciscan church shelters the tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli beneath Giotto's softly fading frescoes. Save time for the cloister and Brunelleschi's serene Pazzi Chapel, a masterclass in Renaissance proportion.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets online to skip the ticket-office line, which can snake across the piazza on busy afternoons.

attractions.name: Mercato Centrale
attractions.description: Downstairs is a working 19th-century iron-and-glass market where Florentines haggle over tripe, truffles and porcini; upstairs is a buzzing food hall with pasta, pizza and wine counters open until late. Come early to watch the stalls stack their produce before the crowds arrive.
attractions.hours: Ground-floor market 07:00–14:00 Mon–Sat; upstairs food hall 09:00–midnight daily
attractions.bookingTip: Walk past the leather-stall touts outside and head straight in — the best-value lunches are at the ground-floor tripe and panino counters.

hotels.name: Palazzo delle Nove Lune
hotels.description: A 15th-century merchant's palazzo reborn as 38 frescoed suites, some with windows framing the Ponte Vecchio's jumble of goldsmith shops. The rooftop loggia pours Negronis at sunset, and the spa is carved into the building's medieval foundations.

hotels.name: Casa Tessitori
hotels.description: Twelve rooms in a former silk weavers' workshop, dressed in hand-loomed linens from a Prato mill and antiques hunted down at the Santo Spirito flea market. Breakfast is served in a walled lemon-tree garden two minutes from the Pitti.

hotels.name: Giglio Rosso Social Hostel
hotels.description: Bright dorms and private doubles above a busy market street, with a communal kitchen stocked by daily runs to the Mercato Centrale. The terrace bar hosts cheap family-style pasta nights, the easiest way to meet fellow travellers.

hotels.name: Linea d'Oro Design Hotel
hotels.description: Clean-lined Italian furniture plays against exposed 14th-century beams, with gold-leaf accents crafted by a gilder from the next street. The lobby doubles as a rotating gallery for young Florentine artists.

hotels.name: Villa Poggio dei Cipressi
hotels.description: A cypress-lined 18th-century villa on the hillside above San Niccolò, with a terraced olive grove and a pool that looks straight at Brunelleschi's dome. It feels like deep countryside, yet the river is a 15-minute downhill stroll.

hotels.name: Altana dei Servi Apartments
hotels.description: Self-catering one- and two-bedroom flats on the quiet street linking the Duomo and Santissima Annunziata, each with a full kitchen and washing machine. The shared rooftop altana has a dome view that rivals any paid terrace.

restaurants.name: Il Carretto di Zio Ubaldo
restaurants.description: A green-painted tripe cart on a corner behind the market, where a third-generation trippaio ladles lampredotto straight from a bubbling pot. Order it 'bagnato' so the bread gets a dunk in the broth, then eat standing up with a plastic cup of house red.

restaurants.name: Pasticceria Fior di Sfoglia
restaurants.description: Locals crowd the marble bar for cornetti still warm from the oven and budini di riso, Florence's creamy rice-custard tartlets. Coffee at the counter costs half the table price, so stand like the Florentines do.

restaurants.name: Ottava Stanza
restaurants.description: Hidden in the vaulted rooms of a former guild hall, this 26-seat dining room reworks peasant Tuscan cooking with surgical precision — pappa al pomodoro reimagined as a chilled, crystal-clear consommé. The cellar leans hard on small Chianti Classico and Montalcino growers.
restaurants.signatureDish: Roast pigeon with Vin Santo and chestnut

restaurants.name: Trattoria Le Tre Pentole
restaurants.description: Checked tablecloths, a wood-fired grill and a handwritten menu that shifts with the seasons make this the perfect dinner after walking down from the sunset crowds. The bistecca is cut to order and presented raw at your table before it meets the embers.

restaurants.name: Osteria del Chiodo Storto
restaurants.description: A bent nail hangs above the door of this cramped Oltrarno osteria, where three pastas are chalked on a board each day and ribollita arrives in chipped terracotta bowls. Expect shared tables, house wine by the carafe and staff happy to translate the Italian-only menu.

restaurants.name: Vinaino della Buca Stretta
restaurants.description: This pocket-sized enoteca has revived one of Florence's historic buchette del vino, the little stone hatches once used to sell wine straight onto the street. Order a glass through the window, or duck inside for chicken-liver crostini and a Chianti Classico tasting flight.

restaurants.name: Sesamo Nero
restaurants.description: When you've had your fill of pecorino, this bright mezze bar near the Sant'Ambrogio market serves smoky baba ganoush, herb-flecked falafel and flatbreads baked to order. Most dishes are plant-based, making it a rare vegan haven in steak country.

restaurants.name: Pizzeria Forno Brace
restaurants.description: A tiled wood-fired oven, blistered 48-hour dough and buffalo mozzarella trucked up from Campania make this the best pizza stop near the David. It stays open late, handy after an evening church concert.

experiences.name: Dawn Uffizi Masterpieces with an Art Historian
experiences.description: Beat the tour-group crush with the first entry of the day and a PhD art historian who decodes Botticelli, Leonardo and Caravaggio in plain, witty English. The route is timed to reach the Birth of Venus before the crowds do.

experiences.name: Market-to-Table Pici and Tiramisù Class
experiences.description: Shop the market stalls with a Florentine home cook, then climb to a nearby kitchen to hand-roll fat pici noodles, simmer a seasonal sauce and whip up tiramisù. It all ends with a long lunch and the recipes sent to your inbox.

experiences.name: Chianti Hills by Vintage Fiat 500
experiences.description: Convoy along cypress-lined Chianti backroads in restored 1960s Fiat 500s, following a lead car with walkie-talkies so nobody gets lost. Stops include a family winery cellar tour and tasting plus a farmhouse lunch overlooking the vines; drivers need a licence and some manual-gearbox confidence.

experiences.name: Oltrarno Aperitivo and Wine-Window Crawl
experiences.description: Cross the Ponte Vecchio at golden hour and hop between four Oltrarno haunts with a local sommelier, pairing Tuscan wines with crostini, finocchiona and aged pecorino. Along the way you'll hear the plague-era story of Florence's wine windows and order a glass through one.
